theme: Harvest-cycle design, stale AI memory & Cloudflare's KV-cache leak

questions.concept: Interpreting lab results before showing raw values
questions.question: A diagnostics app now sends lab reports to patients the moment results are ready, often before the doctor has reviewed them. Support tickets and panicked calls to clinics have spiked. What is the best product change?
options: Delay every report until the doctor has reviewed it, so patients only ever see results that come with a clinician's note attached
Show each result with a plain-language range explanation and what it usually means, and flag which values the doctor will discuss, before the raw table
Keep instant delivery but add a prominent disclaimer at the top telling patients not to interpret results without their doctor
Add an in-app chat with a support agent who can answer questions about any value in the report in real time
rationales: Wrong: it removes a real benefit for everyone to protect some users, and may conflict with patients' right to their own data.
Correct: it fixes the root cause, missing context, while keeping fast access that many patients value.
Wrong: a disclaimer does not reduce anxiety. People still see a red number and still worry.
Wrong: it scales cost with every anxious patient and support agents cannot give medical interpretation anyway.
questions.explanation: The pain is anxiety from numbers without context, not the speed of delivery itself. Pairing each value with its normal range, a plain-language meaning and a 'your doctor will review this' cue keeps the benefit of fast access while removing most of the panic. Blanket delays take away value patients want; disclaimers and agents treat symptoms rather than the cause.
questions.interview_tip: In product sense rounds, show that you separate the trigger (instant delivery) from the real pain (numbers without meaning). Keeping the upside while fixing the downside reads as mature judgement.

questions.concept: Repayment schedules aligned to seasonal farm income
questions.question: A fintech's small-loan product for Indian farmers has much higher defaults than its loans to salaried workers, even though farmers' annual incomes are similar. Interviews show most farmers do repay, just late and in lumps. What should the PM change first?
options: Raise the interest rate for farmer loans to price in the higher default risk compared with salaried borrowers
Offer repayment schedules tied to the crop cycle, with small or zero instalments in lean months and larger ones after harvest
Tighten credit checks for farmers so that only those with the most stable year-round income get approved for loans
Send more frequent SMS and IVR reminders before each monthly due date so farmers remember to pay on time
rationales: Wrong: higher rates make lumps harder to repay and treat a timing problem as pure risk.
Correct: it fits the product to the user's real cash-flow pattern, which interviews show is the cause of late payment.
Wrong: it shrinks the market to avoid a design flaw and excludes the very segment the product is for.
Wrong: reminders help people who forget. These farmers do not forget, they have no cash until harvest.
questions.explanation: The evidence says farmers are willing and able to pay but their cash arrives in lumps after harvest, while the product demands equal monthly instalments. That is a product-user mismatch, not a credit-risk problem. Matching the schedule to when money actually arrives fixes the cause; reminders, pricing and stricter approvals all treat it as an intent or risk issue it is not.
questions.interview_tip: Interviewers reward candidates who read the evidence carefully: 'they repay, just late and in lumps' points to timing, not willingness. Showing you can redesign the product around the user's constraints is a strong signal.

questions.concept: User control over algorithmic feed ordering
questions.question: Users of a team-updates app complain that since the feed became ranked by relevance, they miss time-sensitive posts from their own manager. Engagement overall is up. What is the most sensible response?
options: Keep the ranked feed unchanged because the overall engagement increase proves it is serving users better
Keep ranked as the default but let users switch to a 'latest' view and always pin posts from people they report to
Revert the whole feed to chronological order for everyone, since the complaints show ranking is not working
Send users a weekly email digest of every manager post so they can catch up on anything the feed hid
rationales: Wrong: aggregate engagement can rise while an important job, seeing your manager's posts, gets worse.
Correct: it keeps the engagement gains and fixes the specific failure with user control and a clear rule.
Wrong: it discards a change that works for most users to fix one case that can be handled directly.
Wrong: time-sensitive content needs to be seen when it matters, not days later in an email.
questions.explanation: Ranking helps most users browse, but some content has a must-see property that relevance models miss. Giving users a chronological option and hard rules for critical relationships keeps the gains while restoring trust. Reverting throws away the benefit; ignoring the complaints lets a real failure persist; a weekly digest arrives too late for time-sensitive posts.
questions.interview_tip: A good answer protects the majority win and solves the edge case precisely. Candidates who jump to 'revert' or 'ignore' signal all-or-nothing thinking.

questions.concept: Trusted-contact alerts to protect older users from scams
questions.question: A UPI payments app sees that users over 65 lose far more money to phone scams, where a caller persuades them to send a large payment to a 'bank official'. Older users strongly dislike being locked out of their own money. What should the PM build?
options: A hard daily payment limit for all users over 65 that can only be raised by visiting a bank branch in person
An AI model that silently blocks any payment it scores as a likely scam without telling the user why
An optional trusted-contact feature: unusual large payments pause briefly and notify a family member the user chose, who can call them before it goes through
A pop-up warning on every payment for users over 65 reminding them that banks never ask customers to transfer money
rationales: Wrong: it treats every older user as incapable, is paternalistic, and makes legitimate large payments painful.
Wrong: silent blocks with no explanation create false positives users cannot fix and destroy trust.
Correct: it targets the scam mechanism (isolation and urgency) while keeping the user in control.
Wrong: warnings on every payment become noise, and scammers often tell victims to ignore exactly these messages.
questions.explanation: Scams work by isolating the victim in the moment; a short pause plus a call from someone they trust breaks that pressure. Making it opt-in and limited to unusual payments respects autonomy, which older users clearly care about. Hard limits and silent blocks remove control; warnings on every payment cause warning fatigue and are ignored when a scammer is coaching the victim.
questions.interview_tip: Strong candidates name the attacker's tactic (isolation, urgency) and design against it while respecting the user's dignity. Balancing safety and autonomy explicitly is what top-tier interviewers look for.

questions.concept: Day-boundary shift in daily metric reporting
questions.question: After the data team moved the warehouse's daily cut-off from IST midnight to UTC midnight, an Indian food-delivery app's dashboard shows dinner orders falling 20% and lunch orders rising. Total weekly orders are unchanged. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Restaurants started closing earlier in the evening, which reduced the number of dinner orders customers could place
Customers are shifting their ordering from dinner to lunch, probably because of a seasonal change in eating habits
A pricing change made lunch cheaper than dinner, nudging price-sensitive customers to move their orders earlier
Orders are now bucketed by UTC hour and day, so evening IST orders are labelled as earlier hours and the meal splits shifted without any real change
rationales: Wrong: early closing would lower total orders, but the weekly total did not move.
Wrong: a real behaviour shift would not coincide exactly with a data change, and nothing else supports it.
Wrong: no pricing change was mentioned, and you should not invent causes that the facts do not support.
Correct: the timing matches the pipeline change and the total is unchanged, which points to a reporting artefact.
questions.explanation: UTC is five and a half hours behind IST, so an 8:30 PM IST dinner order is stamped 3:00 PM UTC. If meal-time buckets and day boundaries now follow UTC, dinner orders get counted in earlier buckets and late-night orders move to the previous day. The tell is that the weekly total is flat and the change lines up exactly with a pipeline change. Always rule out definition changes before inventing behavioural stories.
questions.interview_tip: In root-cause questions, interviewers want you to check 'did the measurement change?' first. Mentioning time zones and day boundaries shows real hands-on analytics experience.

questions.concept: Launch confounded by a simultaneous marketing campaign
questions.question: A new onboarding checklist launched to 100% of users on the same day marketing started a large TV campaign. Signups and week-1 activation both rose. The PM wants to credit the checklist with the activation gain. What is the main problem?
options: TV campaigns usually bring lower-quality users, so activation should have fallen and the checklist must have caused the rise
The campaign changed who signed up at the same time, so the activation gain cannot be separated from the checklist without a holdout or other comparison
The checklist only affects users who complete it, so activation should be measured among completers to see its real effect
Activation is a lagging metric, so it is too early to judge any onboarding change after only one week of data
rationales: Wrong: this assumes the campaign's effect on quality without evidence, and uses that guess to 'prove' causation.
Correct: the two causes are confounded, so the effect of the checklist alone cannot be measured.
Wrong: looking only at completers adds selection bias, because motivated users are more likely to complete it.
Wrong: week-1 activation is a reasonable early metric; the issue is attribution, not timing.
questions.explanation: Two changes landed at once, and the campaign changes both the volume and the mix of new users. Any change in activation could come from either. Without a randomised holdout, or a credible comparison such as regions with no campaign, the checklist's effect is not identified. The fix for next time is to keep a holdout on full launches.
questions.interview_tip: Calling out confounding and suggesting a holdout for every launch shows rigour. Interviewers notice candidates who resist taking credit for a metric move they cannot isolate.

questions.concept: Rating inflation compressing star-rating signal
questions.question: On a services marketplace, 92% of reviews are 5 stars and the average provider rating is 4.8. Customers say ratings no longer help them choose. Which change most improves the usefulness of the quality signal?
options: Ask customers to rate providers on a 10-point scale instead of 5, so there is more room for differentiation
Remove all ratings from the marketplace, since they no longer carry any useful information for customers
Show signals with more spread, such as share of customers who would rebook and specific tags like 'on time', instead of relying on the average star rating
Display the average rating to two decimal places so customers can see the small differences between providers
rationales: Wrong: social pressure to give top marks remains, so a 10-point scale usually inflates the same way.
Wrong: ratings still build baseline trust and catch bad providers; the fix is to add better signals.
Correct: it replaces a compressed signal with ones that actually vary between providers.
Wrong: extra decimals mostly show noise, not real quality differences.
questions.explanation: When nearly everyone gives 5 stars, the average is squeezed near the top and stops separating good from great. Behavioural or specific signals, such as rebooking rate or attribute tags, vary more and carry more information. More decimals show noise, a bigger scale tends to inflate the same way, and removing ratings throws away trust.
questions.interview_tip: Rating inflation comes up in marketplace questions. A strong answer names the compression problem and suggests signals with more variance, such as rebook rate.

questions.concept: Metric definition change after merging two apps
questions.question: A company merged its separate chat app into its main social app. After the merge, the main app's DAU rose 30% but average sessions per user and time per session both fell. Leadership asks whether engagement got worse. What is the best first answer?
options: Yes: falling sessions per user and shorter sessions show that each user is getting less value from the merged app
Yes: users clearly dislike the merged experience, so the company should consider separating the apps again
No: a 30% DAU increase is a clear sign of success, so the per-user metrics can be ignored for now
Not necessarily: the user base and what counts as a session changed, so compare the combined users' behaviour across both apps before and after
rationales: Wrong: averages fell partly because a different mix of users and session types now counts.
Wrong: it jumps to a big decision from metrics that are not comparable across the change.
Wrong: DAU also rose mechanically from adding the chat app's users, so it is not clean evidence either.
Correct: it recognises that the population and the definitions changed, and proposes an apples-to-apples comparison.
questions.explanation: The merge changed the denominator (chat-only users now count in DAU) and the meaning of a session (quick chat checks are short, frequent sessions). Per-user averages will move even if no one behaves differently. The fair comparison is the same set of people's total engagement across both apps before versus their engagement in the merged app after.
questions.interview_tip: This tests whether you notice that both numerator and denominator changed. Proposing a same-users, before-and-after comparison is the move that impresses interviewers.

questions.concept: External validity of a test run in an atypical period
questions.question: An e-commerce team ran an A/B test on a new 'buy now' layout during the Diwali sale week. It showed a 6% conversion lift. What is the main caution before rolling it out year-round?
options: Sale-week shoppers behave differently from normal-week shoppers, so the lift may not hold in ordinary weeks and should be re-checked
A 6% lift is too large to be real, so the result must be a bug and should be thrown away entirely
The lift is only meaningful if the test is also run during the next Diwali sale to confirm it then
The test is invalid because both groups saw the sale, which means the control group was contaminated by the treatment
rationales: Correct: it raises external validity, whether a valid result for one period carries over to others.
Wrong: large lifts deserve scrutiny, but 6% during a sale is plausible and not by itself evidence of a bug.
Wrong: the question is whether it works in normal weeks, which a second sale-week test would not answer.
Wrong: both groups seeing the sale is fine; that is what keeps the comparison fair within the week.
questions.explanation: Randomisation makes the result internally valid for that week, but the people and their intent during a big sale are unusual: more deal-seekers and more urgency. The effect may be smaller, or even reversed, in a normal week. Re-running or holding back a small group after the sale checks whether it generalises.
questions.interview_tip: Separating internal validity (was the test fair?) from external validity (does it generalise?) shows experimentation maturity.

questions.concept: User-level vs query-level randomization for consistency
questions.question: A search team wants to test a new ranking model. An engineer proposes randomising each search query independently, so the same user might get old ranking on one search and new ranking on the next. What is the main risk?
options: Search queries are not independent events, so standard significance tests cannot be applied to any query-level metric
Users get an inconsistent experience and learn across both versions, which can blur the difference and makes user-level metrics like retention impossible to attribute
Query-level randomisation needs far more traffic than user-level, so the test would take months longer to finish
The ranking model would have to be loaded twice in memory, which doubles serving cost during the experiment
rationales: Wrong: correlation among a user's queries needs adjusted variance, but tests can still be done; that is not the main risk.
Correct: it names both problems, spill-over within a user and the loss of user-level outcome metrics.
Wrong: query-level usually gives more units and more power, not less, which is why engineers propose it.
Wrong: serving cost is an engineering detail, not a validity problem for the experiment.
questions.explanation: With query-level splits, one person experiences both arms. Their behaviour on one search is shaped by the other, and you cannot measure user-level outcomes such as return visits per arm. Query-level splits can be fine for short-term click metrics, but user-level randomisation is needed when consistency and long-term behaviour matter.
questions.interview_tip: Explaining why the randomisation unit should match the metric you care about is a classic signal of experimentation depth.

questions.concept: Annual phone-charger unit sales in India
questions.question: Roughly how many mobile phone chargers are sold in India each year? Use about 700 million smartphone users and assume a typical charger is replaced, lost or supplemented every 2 to 3 years.
options: About 300 million
About 3 billion
About 30 million
About 3 million
rationales: Correct: 700 million users replacing about every 2.5 years gives roughly 280 to 300 million.
Wrong: this would be more than four chargers per user per year, which is not realistic.
Wrong: this implies a charger every 23 years per user, which ignores how often chargers break or get lost.
Wrong: this implies one charger per 230 users a year, far too few for a cheap, often-lost accessory.
questions.explanation: Start with about 700 million users. If each buys a charger roughly every 2.5 years because of breakage, loss, a spare for work or a phone that ships without one, that is 700M / 2.5 = about 280 million a year. Add a little for feature phones and power banks counted separately and you land near 300 million. The order of magnitude is what matters.
questions.interview_tip: State your base, your replacement rate and your result in one line. Interviewers care more about a clear, checkable chain than the exact number.

questions.concept: Annual speech-to-text minutes for a company's meetings
questions.question: A 5,000-person company wants to transcribe all its internal meetings. Employees average 8 hours of meetings a week, meetings average 5 attendees, and there are about 48 working weeks a year. Roughly how many minutes of audio need transcribing per year?
options: About 115 million minutes
About 23 million minutes
About 1.2 billion minutes
About 2.3 million minutes
rationales: Wrong: this counts person-minutes (5,000 x 8 x 48 x 60), transcribing each meeting once per attendee.
Correct: 5,000 x 8 / 5 x 48 x 60 = about 23 million unique meeting minutes.
Wrong: this is ten times the person-minutes figure and far above any realistic meeting load.
Wrong: this is ten times too low, likely from a misplaced zero or using hours per month.
questions.explanation: Person-hours of meetings per week: 5,000 x 8 = 40,000. Each meeting is shared by 5 people, so unique meeting-hours are 40,000 / 5 = 8,000 a week. Over 48 weeks: 384,000 hours, or about 23 million minutes. The common mistake is to skip dividing by attendees, which counts each meeting five times.
questions.interview_tip: Catching the 'shared meeting' double-count shows you sanity-check units. Saying 'person-minutes versus meeting-minutes' out loud earns credit.

questions.concept: Revenue-threshold licensing for open-weight models
questions.question: An AI lab releases small open-weight models that anyone can use free, but companies above $10 million in annual revenue must buy a commercial licence. What is the main strategic logic of this licence?
options: It drives broad adoption by developers and startups for free while capturing revenue from large companies that get the most value and can afford to pay
It lets the lab avoid any liability for how small companies use the models, because they are not paying customers
It prevents large companies from using the models at all, so the lab avoids competing with its biggest potential customers
It keeps the models closed in practice, since most developers will not risk using a model with any licence conditions attached
rationales: Correct: it combines open-source distribution with charging the segment with the highest willingness to pay.
Wrong: liability is not tied to payment in that way, and this is not why such licences exist.
Wrong: large companies can use the models; they just need to pay for a licence.
Wrong: free use below the threshold is designed to encourage wide adoption, not to discourage it.
questions.explanation: Free use for individuals and small firms builds a developer community, integrations and mindshare, which open weights are good at. The revenue threshold is a form of price discrimination: the companies extracting the most value pay, while the funnel stays wide. Startups that grow past the line become paying customers.
questions.interview_tip: Connecting a licence design to distribution and price discrimination shows business sense. Mentioning the 'grow into paying' path is a nice extra.

questions.concept: Third-degree price discrimination via verified segment discounts
questions.question: A music streaming service offers a 50% student discount, but only after verifying enrolment through a third-party service. Why is the verification step essential to the strategy?
options: It is legally required to collect student information before offering any kind of price discount to customers
Without it, full-price users would claim the discount, so the lower price would leak to customers who would have paid more
Verification adds friction that makes students value the subscription more, raising long-term retention
It allows the company to sell student data to advertisers, which covers the cost of the discount
rationales: Wrong: there is no general legal requirement like this; the reason is commercial.
Correct: segment pricing needs a fence; verification stops higher-paying users from taking the discount.
Wrong: friction does not reliably raise perceived value, and that is not the purpose of the step.
Wrong: this is not the logic of the strategy and would create serious privacy and trust problems.
questions.explanation: Charging different groups different prices works only if groups cannot easily switch into the cheaper one. Students tend to have lower willingness to pay; the discount wins them without lowering the price for everyone. Verification is the fence that stops leakage. Without it, the discount just becomes a price cut.
questions.interview_tip: Using the term 'fence' for segment pricing shows you know how price discrimination works in practice.

questions.concept: Entering a market that has already tipped to an incumbent
questions.question: A well-funded startup wants to launch a general-purpose ride-hailing app in a city where one incumbent already has about 85% share, strong network effects and riders who rarely open other apps. Which strategy has the best chance?
options: Find an underserved niche the incumbent handles poorly, such as airport transfers with fixed prices or women-only drivers, and win it first
Launch city-wide with lower prices than the incumbent and fund the losses until riders and drivers switch over
Copy the incumbent's product feature for feature, then outspend it on brand advertising to win mindshare
Wait for the incumbent to make a mistake, then launch quickly to capture the users who are unhappy with it
rationales: Correct: it avoids fighting the incumbent's network advantage head-on and builds density where it can win.
Wrong: the incumbent can match price cuts with its denser network, and users return when subsidies end.
Wrong: parity gives no reason to switch, and brand spend does not overcome a liquidity advantage.
Wrong: waiting is not a strategy; the incumbent may never stumble, and the team burns cash meanwhile.
questions.explanation: Once a network-effect market has tipped, a head-on attack means subsidising both sides against a rival with more density and lower costs. Price wars usually lose unless the challenger has a clearly better cost structure. A niche the incumbent serves badly lets the challenger build local density and a reason to exist, and then expand from strength.
questions.interview_tip: In market-entry questions, naming 'tipped market' and explaining why niche-first beats head-on shows strategic depth. Top candidates also say how they would expand out of the niche.

questions.concept: Dual-write and backfill for an irreversible data migration
questions.question: Your team is moving customer orders from an old database to a new one. Once old records are deleted, the move cannot be undone. Which rollout plan best manages the risk?
options: Write to both databases, backfill old data, compare reads between them, switch reads gradually, and only delete the old store after a stable period
Migrate a random 10% of customers fully to the new database, delete their old records, and then do the rest a week later
Copy everything over a weekend during low traffic, switch to the new database on Monday, and delete the old one to save costs
Keep using the old database for writes forever and only read from the new one for reporting and analytics
rationales: Correct: each step can be reversed until the very last one, which is delayed until the new store is proven.
Wrong: deleting old records for 10% early removes the rollback path for those customers if bugs appear.
Wrong: it is a big-bang move with no fallback if problems show up after Monday.
Wrong: it never finishes the migration and keeps paying for two systems with unclear ownership.
questions.explanation: When the final step cannot be reversed, make every step before it reversible. Dual writes keep both stores current, comparisons catch data mismatches, a gradual read switch limits blast radius, and delaying deletion keeps a rollback path until you are confident. A big-bang weekend cut-over bets everything on one attempt.
questions.interview_tip: Saying 'keep every step reversible until the one-way door' signals strong execution instincts. It is a phrase interviewers at Amazon and Google recognise.

questions.concept: Pseudo-localisation to catch UI issues before translation
questions.question: An app is launching in German and Hindi in eight weeks. Translations will only be ready two weeks before launch. How can the team find text-overflow and hard-coded string problems early?
options: Make every text field auto-shrink its font size so longer translations will always fit without any layout changes
Wait for the real translations and fix any layout problems found in the two weeks before launch
Ask the translation agency to send rough machine translations early so designers can check the screens
Run pseudo-localisation: replace strings with longer, accented placeholder text in test builds to expose truncation and untranslated strings now
rationales: Wrong: auto-shrinking can make text unreadable and does not catch strings that were never externalised.
Wrong: it pushes all discovery into the riskiest two weeks, leaving little time to fix problems.
Wrong: it helps somewhat, but depends on another team and still misses hard-coded strings systematically.
Correct: it surfaces layout and hard-coded string issues weeks early without needing real translations.
questions.explanation: Pseudo-localisation swaps every string for a padded, accented version, often 30 to 40% longer. Anything that truncates, overlaps or stays in plain English shows up immediately, long before real translations arrive. It turns a last-minute scramble into normal work spread across the schedule.
questions.interview_tip: Mentioning pseudo-localisation in an international launch question shows practical delivery experience beyond the basics.

questions.concept: Osborne effect from pre-announcing a product
questions.question: A B2B hardware company plans to announce a much better next-generation device six months before it ships, while still selling the current model. What is the biggest risk?
options: The engineering team will feel pressure to ship on time, which may lead to a lower-quality first release
The sales team will not have enough training on the new device to answer customer questions in time
Competitors will copy the new device before it launches, wiping out the company's technical lead entirely
Customers delay purchases of the current model to wait for the new one, which can sharply cut revenue before the new device ships
rationales: Wrong: deadline pressure is real but secondary to the immediate revenue risk.
Wrong: training is solvable with planning and is not the main strategic risk of announcing early.
Wrong: copying hardware in six months is hard; it is a smaller risk than lost current sales.
Correct: pre-announcing a clearly better product makes buyers wait, cutting current revenue.
questions.explanation: This is the Osborne effect, named after a computer maker whose sales collapsed after it announced a successor too early. Buyers rationally wait, and the current product's sales drop while the new one is not yet available. If you must pre-announce, pair it with upgrade credits or trade-in offers so current buyers are not penalised.
questions.interview_tip: Naming the Osborne effect and offering a mitigation, such as an upgrade guarantee, shows you think about launch timing as a business decision.

questions.concept: Pressure to hide a risk until after someone's promotion
questions.question: A peer PM asks you not to raise a serious launch risk you found in their project at next week's leadership review, saying it would hurt their promotion case and they will 'fix it quietly'. What is the best response?
options: Agree to stay silent this once, since they promised to fix it and raising it would damage a colleague's career
Report the peer's request to HR so the company knows they tried to hide information from leadership
Tell them you will not stay silent, offer to help them raise it themselves with a mitigation plan first, and raise it yourself if they do not
Raise the risk at the leadership review without telling the peer first, since leaders need to hear it directly
rationales: Wrong: silence lets leaders decide on false information, and makes you complicit if the risk materialises.
Wrong: escalating to HR first is out of proportion before even a direct conversation has happened.
Correct: it keeps integrity non-negotiable while giving the peer a fair, dignified way to own it.
Wrong: surprising the peer damages trust when a direct conversation could get the same result better.
questions.explanation: Hiding a serious risk to protect someone's promotion is not acceptable; leaders need accurate information to make decisions. But the best approach also respects the colleague: give them the chance to own the message with a plan, which is better for them too. Be clear that the risk will be raised either way.
questions.interview_tip: Interviewers look for firm integrity paired with empathy. Saying 'I would give them the chance to own it, but it would be raised either way' hits both.

questions.concept: Lending engineers to a company priority at cost to your own goals
questions.question: A company-critical launch on another team is slipping. Their director asks to borrow two of your strongest engineers for six weeks, which would cause you to miss one of your quarterly goals. What is the best way to handle it?
options: Assess the company-level impact with your manager, agree if it is higher, and make the trade-off explicit by resetting your goal in writing
Offer two less critical engineers instead so you can help a little while still hitting your own goals
Decline, because your quarterly goals are your commitment and lending engineers would mean failing your own team
Agree right away without telling your manager, since helping the company should always come first
rationales: Correct: it puts company impact first and makes the cost transparent through your manager.
Wrong: it looks helpful but may not solve the problem the director has, while avoiding a real decision.
Wrong: it puts team goals above a company-critical need without even checking the relative impact.
Wrong: the instinct is good, but hiding the trade-off sets up confusion when your goal is missed.
questions.explanation: Strong PMs optimise for the company, not just their own scorecard. But the decision should be made with the right people and the trade-off made visible, so your missed goal is understood as a choice, not a failure. Quietly agreeing hides the cost; refusing ignores bigger priorities; sending weaker people may not actually help.
questions.interview_tip: Amazon and Google interviewers like answers that show company-first thinking plus explicit trade-offs. 'I reset expectations in writing' is a strong detail.

questions.concept: Rewarding messengers to keep bad news flowing
questions.question: Three months after you pushed hard for a new architecture, a senior engineer privately tells you it is not scaling and the team has been afraid to say so. What is the best first response?
options: Thank them, acknowledge your role in making it hard to speak up, review the evidence together, and openly share the findings with the team
Ask them for detailed data first, since you need to be sure before changing direction on such a major technical decision
Quietly start planning a replacement architecture so the team does not lose confidence in the current direction
Ask why they did not raise it sooner, since three months of work could have been saved if they had spoken up
rationales: Correct: it rewards candour, owns your role and moves to evidence and transparency.
Wrong: data matters, but leading with a demand for proof can feel like pushback and discourages candour.
Wrong: hiding it repeats the original problem and erodes trust when the team finds out.
Wrong: blaming the messenger guarantees people will stay quiet next time.
questions.explanation: How a leader reacts to the first piece of bad news decides whether they hear the next one. Thanking the messenger, owning your part in the silence and dealing with it openly signal that raising problems is safe. Evidence still matters, but leading with 'prove it' or 'why so late?' teaches people to stay quiet.
questions.interview_tip: Behavioural answers about bad news are really about psychological safety. Saying you owned your part in the silence signals self-awareness.

questions.concept: Embedding dimensionality vs storage and retrieval quality
questions.question: A team's semantic search stores 500 million documents with 3,072-dimension embeddings. Vector storage cost is now their biggest bill. The embedding model supports shortened vectors. What is the best next step?
options: Remove half of the documents from the index so that storage costs fall without changing the embedding size
Keep full-size embeddings, because any reduction in dimensions will always noticeably hurt retrieval quality
Switch immediately to the smallest available dimension, since shorter vectors are always good enough for search
Evaluate retrieval quality at smaller dimensions such as 768 or 1,024 on their own queries and pick the smallest size that keeps recall acceptable
rationales: Wrong: dropping content hurts coverage and does not address the cost per stored vector.
Wrong: modest reductions often lose little quality; refusing to test leaves big savings on the table.
Wrong: quality loss varies by domain; going straight to the smallest size risks an unmeasured drop.
Correct: it makes the trade-off measurable on real queries and chooses the cheapest acceptable option.
questions.explanation: Storage and search cost scale with dimensions, so a 3x to 4x reduction can save a lot. Many embedding models keep most of their quality at lower sizes, but how much is lost depends on the domain. Measuring recall on your own queries finds the best point on the cost-quality curve instead of guessing.
questions.interview_tip: Treating model choices as a measurable cost-quality curve shows you can partner well with ML engineers.

questions.concept: Stale long-term memory in AI assistants
questions.question: An AI assistant remembers facts users mention, like 'I'm vegetarian' or 'I work at Acme'. Months later, users complain it keeps recommending things based on details that are no longer true. What is the best fix?
options: Turn off memory entirely, since outdated information will always eventually cause the assistant to make mistakes
Ask users to manually re-enter all their personal details every month so that the memory stays current
Let new statements override older memories, show users what is remembered, and age out or re-confirm time-sensitive facts
Keep every memory forever but lower the assistant's temperature so it relies less on remembered information
rationales: Wrong: it throws away a valued feature to fix a design flaw that can be handled.
Wrong: it puts heavy, repetitive work on users and most will not do it.
Correct: it handles updates, transparency and time-sensitivity, the three causes of stale memory.
Wrong: temperature controls randomness, not which memories the assistant trusts.
questions.explanation: Memory is useful but facts about people change. Good memory design treats memories as having a lifespan: newer statements win, users can see and edit what is stored, and facts likely to change (job, location) are re-checked over time. That keeps the value of personalisation without the cost of stale assumptions.
questions.interview_tip: Talking about memory freshness and user control shows you think about AI features over months of use, not just the first session.

questions.concept: Extractive answers for high-stakes policy content
questions.question: An internal HR assistant answers questions about leave and benefits policy. Legal is worried that paraphrased answers sometimes change the meaning of policy wording. What design best addresses this?
options: Remove the assistant and send employees a link to the full policy PDF whenever they ask a question
Show the exact policy passage as the main answer, with a short plain-language summary clearly marked and linked to the source
Have the model paraphrase more carefully by adding instructions in the prompt to never change any policy meaning
Use a larger, more capable model so that its paraphrases are more accurate and less likely to change meaning
rationales: Wrong: it removes the value of quick answers and sends people back to searching long documents.
Correct: the authoritative text is what users see, and the summary is a clearly labelled aid.
Wrong: prompt instructions help but cannot guarantee that meaning is never changed.
Wrong: better models paraphrase better, but still do not give the legal certainty that quoting does.
questions.explanation: When exact wording has legal weight, the safest answer is extractive: quote the source text and treat any summary as a helper, clearly labelled. That keeps the convenience of fast answers while making the authoritative text the thing users rely on. Prompting and bigger models reduce errors but cannot guarantee faithful paraphrase.
questions.interview_tip: Knowing when to choose extractive over generative answers shows you match AI design to risk, a key theme in AI PM interviews.

questions.concept: Risk-stratified human review sampling for AI outputs
questions.question: A bank's AI drafts 50,000 customer replies a day. The QA team can review only 1,000. Errors on dispute and fraud replies are far costlier than on general queries. How should the PM allocate reviews?
options: Review only dispute and fraud replies, since general queries are low risk and do not need any human checking
Review only the 1,000 replies with the lowest model confidence scores, since those are the most likely to contain errors
Sample heavily from high-risk categories and low-confidence outputs, plus a smaller random sample of everything, and weight error-rate estimates accordingly
Review a simple random 2% sample of all replies so that the measured error rate represents the full population fairly
rationales: Wrong: it leaves general queries unchecked, so new failure types there would go unnoticed.
Wrong: models are often confidently wrong; this misses high-confidence errors completely.
Correct: it focuses on risk and uncertainty while keeping an unbiased random baseline.
Wrong: it gives a fair overall rate but spends most reviews on low-stakes replies and misses rare costly ones.
questions.explanation: Limited review capacity should go where errors cost most and are most likely. But you still need a random slice of everything to catch failures in areas you assumed were safe and to estimate the overall error rate without bias. Weighting by sampling rate corrects the estimate. Pure random sampling wastes reviews on low-risk replies; pure confidence or category targeting leaves blind spots.
questions.interview_tip: Combining risk-based targeting with a random baseline shows statistical and product judgement together, a strong signal for AI PM roles.

questions.concept: Error propagation from upstream OCR in document AI
questions.question: An invoice-processing AI extracts amounts from scanned PDFs, then an LLM checks them against purchase orders. Mismatch flags are frequent, but on inspection most invoices are actually fine. Where should the team look first?
options: At the purchase order database, since it probably contains many wrong amounts that need correction
At the LLM prompt, since the model is clearly bad at comparing two numbers and needs better instructions
At the user interface, since reviewers may be misreading the flags and marking correct invoices as fine
At the OCR step, since misread digits or columns upstream would make the LLM compare wrong numbers and raise false mismatches
rationales: Wrong: possible, but reviewers found the invoices were fine, which points to extraction, not records.
Wrong: comparing two numbers is easy for the LLM; it is likely being given wrong inputs.
Wrong: the reviewers' checks are the evidence that flags are wrong, not the source of the problem.
Correct: upstream extraction errors are a common cause of downstream false alarms.
questions.explanation: In a pipeline, the final step's errors often come from earlier steps. If OCR misreads a digit, the LLM correctly flags a mismatch between the wrong number and the purchase order. Checking intermediate outputs, here the extracted values against the scans, locates the failing step before you tune the wrong component.
questions.interview_tip: Saying 'inspect intermediate outputs to localise the failing step' shows systems thinking about AI pipelines.

questions.concept: Consistent hashing to minimise cache remapping
questions.question: A team spreads cached data across 10 servers by using 'key hash modulo 10'. When they added an 11th server during a traffic spike, almost every cache lookup missed and the database was overloaded. What technique avoids this?
options: Larger servers instead of more servers, so the number of cache servers never has to change at all
A shorter cache expiry time, so that stale entries are cleared out faster after the change
Consistent hashing, so adding a server only moves a small share of keys instead of reshuffling almost all of them
Encrypting cache keys before hashing them, so that keys spread more evenly across all servers
rationales: Wrong: vertical scaling has limits and does not fix the remapping problem when you eventually add servers.
Wrong: shorter expiry adds more misses, making the database load worse, not better.
Correct: it limits key movement when servers change, keeping most of the cache valid.
Wrong: hash functions already spread keys evenly; the issue is remapping, not distribution.
questions.explanation: With modulo hashing, changing the number of servers changes where almost every key lives, so the cache effectively empties at the worst moment. Consistent hashing places servers and keys on a ring, so adding one server only takes over about 1/N of the keys. Most of the cache stays warm.
questions.interview_tip: PMs do not need to implement it, but explaining why a scaling step caused an outage shows strong technical fluency.

questions.concept: Per-key message ordering in queues
questions.question: An order system publishes 'created', 'paid' and 'shipped' events to a message queue processed by many workers in parallel. Sometimes 'shipped' is processed before 'paid', causing errors. What is the standard fix?
options: Process all events with a single worker so that the system handles every event in the exact order it arrived
Ask the team publishing events to send them more slowly so the queue has time to keep them in order
Partition events by order ID so all events for one order go to the same partition and are processed in sequence
Add a random delay before processing 'shipped' events so that the 'paid' events usually arrive first
rationales: Wrong: it works but throws away scale, creating a bottleneck for the whole system.
Wrong: slowing producers is fragile and limits throughput without guaranteeing order.
Correct: it gives ordering where it matters (per order) without losing parallelism.
Wrong: delays reduce but do not prevent misordering, and add latency to every event.
questions.explanation: Most systems only need ordering within one entity, not across everything. Routing every event for the same order ID to the same partition keeps that order's events in sequence while different orders still run in parallel. A single worker gives total order but kills throughput; delays are fragile hacks.
questions.interview_tip: Knowing that ordering is usually needed 'per key, not globally' is the kind of insight that helps PMs make good trade-offs with engineers.

questions.concept: Self-referral fraud in referral programmes
questions.question: A quick-commerce app's 'give Rs 100, get Rs 100' referral programme shows a spike in referrals, but many new accounts place one order using the credit and never return. Several share the same device or payment card. What is happening and what should the PM do?
options: New users dislike the app after one order, so the PM should improve the first-order experience to raise retention
The referral programme is working well, since more referrals mean more new customers, so the incentive should be increased
The Rs 100 credit is too small to keep users, so the app should increase it to Rs 250 to encourage repeat orders
Users are referring themselves with new accounts; add device, payment and address checks, and pay the referrer only after the new user's second order
rationales: Wrong: shared devices and cards point to fake accounts, not unhappy genuine users.
Wrong: referral volume without retained users is not growth; bigger incentives fund more fraud.
Wrong: a larger credit makes self-referral more profitable, making the problem worse.
Correct: it names the fraud pattern and both detects it and changes rewards so it is no longer profitable.
questions.explanation: Shared devices and cards across 'new' accounts that order once are classic self-referral signs. The fix is to detect duplicate identities and tie rewards to real value, such as a second order, so fraud stops paying. Raising the incentive would increase fraud, and the problem is not first-order experience.
questions.interview_tip: Growth interviewers like candidates who check incentive programmes for abuse. Tying rewards to a value event shows strong instincts.

questions.concept: Cross-tenant KV-cache exposure (Cloudflare GLM-5.3, Oct 2026)
questions.question: In October 2026 Cloudflare disclosed that between 27 August and 9 September, 155 responses from the GLM-5.3 model on Workers AI contained data from other customers' requests. What did it identify as the cause?
options: A configuration mismatch triggered a bug in the SGLang inference engine that exposed KV-cache pages across requests
An attacker used prompt injection to make the model reveal other users' conversations stored in its training data
The model had been fine-tuned on customer data, so it memorised and repeated other customers' prompts
A misconfigured logging system published customer prompts to a publicly accessible storage bucket
rationales: Correct: this matches Cloudflare's disclosure of an SGLang bug exposing KV-cache pages across requests.
Wrong: there was no reported attacker; it was a serving bug, not prompt injection.
Wrong: no training on customer data was involved; the leak came from cached state at serving time.
Wrong: the issue was inside the inference engine, not a logging or storage misconfiguration.
questions.explanation: Reports of Cloudflare's write-up say a configuration mismatch for GLM-5.3 triggered an SGLang bug that let cached attention state (KV-cache pages) from one request leak into another, with no evidence of deliberate exploitation. Affected responses involved very long prompts. For AI PMs the lesson is that serving optimisations like caching are part of the trust boundary: tenant isolation needs explicit tests, especially on rare paths like very long contexts.
questions.interview_tip: Using a real incident to explain why inference optimisations need isolation testing shows you understand AI infrastructure risk, not just model quality.
